paragraphs: Decision trees are often trained using rules that make convenient choices along the way, which can leave the final tree short of the best solution. This paper instead formulates training as a mixed-integer optimization problem. It targets binary classification trees whose splits can combine several input features, allowing more flexible decision boundaries.

The proposed formulation builds on a support vector machine model using a 1-norm. The authors also introduce techniques, including cutting planes, that strengthen the relaxed optimization problem and shorten the time needed to reach optimality. This matters because the usefulness of explicitly optimizing an entire tree depends partly on whether the resulting computation is manageable.

Across 36 datasets from the UCI repository, the authors report around a 10% improvement in mean testing accuracy over methods from the literature. For larger datasets, they additionally use linear programming to select a training subset. Their numerical results support both the formulation's generalization performance and the usefulness of this data-selection approach for improving mean accuracy at larger scales.
neurips-2020-a-scalable-mip-based-method.tldr: A mixed-integer formulation and data-selection method make optimal multivariate decision-tree training more scalable while improving reported testing accuracy.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search seeks effective network designs, but evaluating candidate networks can be expensive. Sample-based search focuses computation on promising candidates and offers reliable evaluations. One-shot search reduces costs by sharing weights across many architectures, although sharing among very different networks can make their evaluations less reliable. BONAS aims to combine the strengths of these approaches.

The method uses Bayesian optimization to guide the search, with a graph convolutional network predicting candidate performance. At each iteration, it selects several related architectures. Those candidates then share weights during simultaneous training, reducing the computation required to evaluate the selected group. The relationship among candidates is central to the design, rather than an incidental property of the search.

The authors report that this restricted form of sharing substantially accelerates sample-based search while preserving its reliability. Their explanation is that related architectures can share weights more reliably than the diverse architectures used in one-shot search. Experiments against numerous competing methods support the framework's effectiveness, connecting computational savings to a more selective use of weight sharing.
neurips-2020-bridging-the-gap-between-sa.tldr: BONAS accelerates architecture search by using Bayesian optimization to select related networks that can share weights more reliably.

paragraphs: Compositional generalization means learning rules for combining familiar pieces and applying those rules systematically to unfamiliar combinations. The paper addresses difficulties that existing deep learning models have with this ability. Its proposed Neural-Symbolic Stack Machine, or NeSS, brings together a neural sequence model and a symbolic mechanism capable of recursive computation.

The neural component produces execution traces: sequences of instructions that the symbolic stack machine carries out. The machine also includes operations for manipulating sequences. This arrangement gives the neural model responsibility for generating the computation while supplying an explicit execution mechanism with support for recursion. The system learns without training labels that specify the correct execution traces.

The authors report 100% generalization performance in evaluations spanning four domains: SCAN navigation instructions, few-shot compositional instructions, compositional machine translation, and context-free grammar parsing. These results show that the combined architecture successfully handled the tested generalization cases across several kinds of structured sequence tasks. The finding supports pairing neural sequence generation with symbolic execution as an approach to systematic recombination.
neurips-2020-compositional-generalizatio.tldr: NeSS combines neural instruction generation with a symbolic stack machine and reports perfect generalization in evaluations across four compositional domains.

paragraphs: Matching two 3D point clouds means identifying which points correspond, even when the shapes deform. This paper develops a fully differentiable pipeline for dense matching using the functional maps framework. Its central change is to learn the representation basis from data, replacing the fixed Laplace-Beltrami eigenfunctions commonly used in earlier approaches.

The learned basis places points in a higher-dimensional embedding space. Following the functional map approach, the transformation between these representations is linear. A separate architecture learns descriptor functions that help estimate that transformation. Learning both the basis and the descriptors makes the complete correspondence pipeline trainable end to end, allowing both components to adapt to the matching problem.

The authors find that forcing embeddings into a shared canonical form produces worse results. This observation suggests that allowing an extra linear transformation gives the embedding network useful flexibility and greater robustness. They also report state-of-the-art results on challenging non-rigid point-cloud correspondence applications. Together, these findings support learning representations whose alignment remains flexible rather than requiring identical coordinates across shapes.
neurips-2020-correspondence-learning-via.tldr: Learning both embeddings and descriptors improves non-rigid 3D correspondence, with results suggesting that flexible linear alignment helps robustness.

paragraphs: Adding layers increases a Transformer's capacity, but using large or variable depths effectively creates a training challenge. This paper treats layer selection as something the model can learn probabilistically. It learns posterior distributions over which layers to use, making the selection of depth part of the modeling framework.

The authors extend this idea to multilingual translation by training one shared Transformer with a different layer-selection posterior for each language pair. This lets language pairs use the shared network through different selections of layers. The method also alleviates vanishing gradients, enabling stable training of very deep Transformers, including an example with 100 layers.

Evaluations on English-German translation and masked language modeling show improvements over existing approaches for training deeper Transformers. In multilingual experiments, the authors report improvements across the evaluated language pairs for both many-to-one and one-to-many translation. These findings suggest that learning how layers are used can help turn additional model capacity into useful performance, while also addressing a training difficulty associated with depth.
neurips-2020-deep-transformers-with-late.tldr: Probabilistic layer selection stabilizes deep Transformer training and improves the evaluated language-modeling and translation tasks.

paragraphs: Verifying adversarial robustness requires proving that a network meets a specified robustness condition. The paper argues that binarized neural networks make exact verification substantially more efficient while retaining comparable robustness. It addresses two difficulties with verification of real-valued networks: the cost of complete verification and correctness concerns arising from floating-point arithmetic.

The proposed EEV system combines a specialized SAT solver with training strategies that make networks easier to verify. The solver directly handles the counting constraints produced by binarized network encodings. Training promotes balanced sparsity across layers and low cardinality bounds, and adaptively cancels gradients. The network and verification procedure are therefore designed together to improve tractability.

The authors report exact verification of robustness against bounded changes under the L-infinity measure for nontrivial convolutional binarized networks on MNIST and CIFAR10. Against real-valued networks with the same architectures and tasks, EEV is hundreds to thousands of times faster. Verifiable accuracy remains comparable in most cases, indicating substantial verification savings without a corresponding large loss in that measured outcome across most comparisons.
neurips-2020-efficient-exact-verificatio.tldr: EEV combines specialized solving and verification-friendly training to verify binarized networks exactly, with large reported speedups and usually comparable verifiable accuracy.

paragraphs: A standard model of environment dynamics predicts a single step into the future. The gamma-model instead represents the future over an infinite probabilistic horizon. This changes what a dynamics model contains: long-term information becomes part of the learned prediction, rather than something obtained only by repeatedly applying a one-step model.

The model is trained through a generative interpretation of temporal difference learning. The authors describe it as a continuous analogue of the successor representation and a combination of model-free and model-based mechanisms. Like a value function, it captures information about the distant future. Like a predictive dynamics model, it remains independent of the reward associated with a particular task.

Replacing one-step models with gamma-models leads to generalized procedures for model rollout and value estimation. The paper implements the idea using both generative adversarial networks and normalizing flows, and empirically studies prediction and control. It also identifies an unavoidable tradeoff involving compounding errors during training and testing, making the placement of prediction error a central consideration in learning long-horizon models.
neurips-2020-gamma-models-generative-tem.tldr: Gamma-models learn reward-independent, long-horizon predictions through generative temporal difference learning, connecting model-based and model-free mechanisms.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks combine information from neighboring nodes using coefficients shared throughout a graph. Because those coefficients do not depend on a particular graph, the same learned parameters can potentially be used on another graph. This paper investigates the mathematical basis for that possibility by studying how network outputs relate across graph representations.

The authors introduce graphon neural networks as limiting objects for graph neural networks. They then bound the difference between a finite graph network's output and the output of its graphon limit. This supplies a way to analyze transfer through a common limiting representation, rather than relying solely on the fact that the same coefficients can be reused.

The bound approaches zero as the number of nodes grows when the convolutional filters are bandlimited in the graph spectral domain. That filter condition is central to the stated result. The analysis establishes a tradeoff between transferability and discriminability: restricting spectral behavior supports transfer, while the ability to distinguish graph information is also affected. Parameter sharing alone therefore does not describe the full transferability question.
neurips-2020-graphon-neural-networks-and.tldr: Graphon limits yield a conditional transferability bound for graph neural networks and expose a tradeoff with discriminability.

paragraphs: Recommender systems often learn from feedback that is missing in a selective way. The observed data therefore provide an uneven view of the responses a system would like to predict. Many counterfactual learning methods rely on randomized trials to address this problem, but collecting such data can be extremely expensive in practice.

The paper proposes the counterfactual variational information bottleneck, or CVIB, as a way to reduce learning bias without randomized trials. It separates the task-related mutual information term in an information bottleneck objective into factual and counterfactual components. From that separation, the authors derive a contrastive information loss and an additional penalty on output confidence.

These terms encourage more balanced learning between factual and counterfactual domains, connecting an information-theoretic formulation to an actionable training objective. Evaluations on real-world datasets show significant improvements for both shallow and deep models. The findings support CVIB as an alternative approach to counterfactual recommendation learning when randomized feedback is unavailable or costly, with evidence spanning more than one class of model.
neurips-2020-information-theoretic-count.tldr: CVIB uses an information-theoretic objective to reduce bias from selectively observed recommendation feedback without requiring randomized trials.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether increasing a language model's size improves its ability to perform tasks from a few examples supplied in text. The authors train GPT-3, an autoregressive language model with 175 billion parameters, and evaluate it in this few-shot setting. Their central finding is that scaling substantially improves task-agnostic few-shot performance.

For every evaluated task, the model receives the task description and demonstrations through text interaction. Its parameters are not updated, and it undergoes no task-specific fine-tuning. This setup makes the demonstrations part of the input used to produce an answer, showing how a single trained model can be directed toward different tasks through the same interaction mechanism.

GPT-3 performs strongly on many language datasets, including translation, question answering, and cloze tasks. In some cases, its few-shot performance becomes competitive with earlier state-of-the-art fine-tuning approaches. The authors also identify datasets where it struggles and methodological issues associated with training on large web corpora. The results establish substantial few-shot capability while retaining clear qualifications about its consistency and evaluation.
neurips-2020-language-models-are-few-sho.tldr: GPT-3 shows that scaling language models can substantially improve few-shot task performance using text demonstrations without parameter updates.

paragraphs: Job-shop scheduling often relies on priority dispatching rules to decide which operation should proceed next. Designing effective rules requires substantial specialist knowledge, and the resulting rules can still perform poorly. This paper replaces manual rule design with an end-to-end deep reinforcement learning agent that learns a scheduling policy from scratch.

The approach represents the scheduling problem as a disjunctive graph and uses a graph neural network to encode the states encountered while constructing a schedule. The resulting policy network is size-agnostic: its design is not tied to one fixed instance size. This provides a mechanism for applying a learned dispatching policy to larger scheduling problems.

Experiments show that the agent learns high-quality dispatching rules using elementary raw features and performs strongly against the best existing priority rules considered. The learned policies also work well on much larger instances absent from training. These findings matter because they connect automated rule discovery with practical reuse across problem sizes, reducing dependence on hand-designed scheduling expertise in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2020-learning-to-dispatch-for-jo.tldr: A graph-based reinforcement learning agent learns strong scheduling rules that also perform well on much larger unseen job-shop instances.

paragraphs: Online learners must adapt as data arrive, potentially in arbitrary sequences. Even when the overall prediction problem is complex, particular regions can have useful regularities. This paper develops efficient algorithms that exploit such local structure while comparing their performance with rich classes of functions capable of fitting complicated environments.

A shared master algorithm supports adaptations to three different properties: local smoothness of the comparator function, local metric dimension of the observed instances, and local predictor performance. The algorithms grow hierarchical nets that organize the input space at different resolutions. Pruning those hierarchies produces different descriptions of where finer or coarser treatment is useful.

A tree-expert technique lets the learner efficiently compete with all these prunings at once. The authors prove regret bounds that depend on the relevant form of local regularity. For simple locality profiles, the bounds improve significantly on the earlier approach. Their dependence on time is also no worse than bounds that ignore local regularity, supporting adaptation without worsening that aspect of the guarantee.
neurips-2020-locally-adaptive-nonparamet.tldr: Hierarchical online learners exploit local regularity to improve regret guarantees while preserving the time dependence of bounds that ignore it.

paragraphs: Boosted classifiers often work well with relatively little fine-tuning, and their success is commonly explained through margins. A generalization bound connects properties of a trained classifier to expectations about performance beyond its training data. This paper examines whether an influential margin-based bound actually explains the behavior of modern gradient boosting methods.

The authors show that the existing kth-margin bound is inadequate for explaining the performance of state-of-the-art gradient boosters. This is significant because that bound had been shown to be nearly tight for some data distributions. Being difficult to improve in certain cases does not by itself make a bound an adequate account of the methods performing well in practice.

The paper analyzes the shortcomings and proves a stronger, more refined margin-based generalization bound that does explain the performance under study. It also improves an existing generalization lower bound. The contribution therefore refines the mathematical explanation of boosting: the inadequacy of the earlier margin account leads to a more informative margin-based analysis, rather than abandoning that analytical framework.
neurips-2020-margins-are-insufficient-fo.tldr: The paper shows why an existing margin bound fails to explain modern gradient boosting and proves a stronger, more informative bound.

paragraphs: A generated 3D mesh needs more than accurate geometry to behave usefully in rendering, simulation, or printing. Its surface structure also matters. This paper introduces NeuralMeshFlow to generate two-manifold meshes for genus-zero shapes, addressing the poor manifoldness that the authors identify in earlier methods despite their geometric accuracy.

NeuralMeshFlow is a shape autoencoder that begins with a spherical mesh and progressively deforms it through several neural ordinary differential equation blocks. This gives shape generation a structured starting surface and a sequence of learned deformations. Training does not require explicit mesh-based regularization, which the authors describe as making it simpler than state-of-the-art alternatives.

The experiments demonstrate applications including reconstruction from a single view, global shape parameterization, texture mapping, deformation, and correspondence. They also show that the resulting manifold meshes are better suited to physically based rendering and simulation than those from prior work. The stated genus-zero scope is important: the method targets shapes compatible with its spherical starting structure, and its contribution connects learned geometry with usable surface organization.
neurips-2020-neural-mesh-flow-3d-manifol.tldr: NeuralMeshFlow learns to deform spherical meshes into genus-zero manifold shapes that better support the evaluated rendering and simulation applications.

paragraphs: Adaptive attacks evaluate an adversarial defense by tailoring the attack to that defense. Although this has become a standard evaluation approach, the paper finds that typical adaptive evaluations can still be incomplete. The authors circumvent 13 recently published defenses spanning a diverse range of strategies, despite those defenses having attempted adaptive evaluation.

The paper emphasizes the methodology used to develop the attacks, going beyond reporting that defenses fail. It lays out how an evaluation must be adapted to the particular defense being examined. Some attack strategies carry over across defenses, but no single strategy was sufficient to defeat all the defenses in this study.

The authors consequently argue that adaptive evaluation requires careful, defense-specific tuning and cannot simply be automated. The practical significance is that describing an evaluation as adaptive does not establish that it has adequately challenged the defense. By explaining the attack process, the analyses aim to guide stronger evaluations and help subsequent robustness research distinguish protective behavior from weaknesses left unexplored by the chosen attack.
neurips-2020-on-adaptive-attacks-to-adve.tldr: By circumventing 13 defenses, the paper shows that adaptive attack evaluations can remain incomplete and require careful defense-specific tuning.

paragraphs: The paper examines a claim that number sense emerges spontaneously in a neural network trained only to recognize visual objects. The authors challenge the statistical evidence for that claim. They identify a mismatch between the small sample used to find number-sensitive neurons and the very large number of neurons examined.

According to their analysis, the same flawed procedure can identify apparently number-sensitive neurons in randomly initialized networks that have never been trained. This makes the statistical procedure central to the dispute: finding such neurons under that test does not establish that object-recognition training produced number sense. The authors then investigate networks deliberately trained on images depicting numbers.

Those follow-up findings are mixed. Even with explicit numerosity training, the networks have difficulty acquiring an abstract concept of number. At the same time, the authors find encouraging evidence that the networks handle distribution shifts more robustly for small numbers than for large ones. The paper thus combines a critique of an earlier inference with a qualified account of what targeted training achieves.
neurips-2020-on-numerosity-of-deep-neura.tldr: The paper rejects flawed evidence for spontaneously learned number sense and finds mixed results when networks are explicitly trained for numerosity.

paragraphs: Optimal transport distances are widely used as learning objectives, but computing them for general probability distributions remains challenging. This paper introduces an online estimator for entropy-regularized optimal transport between two distributions that need not be discrete. Its input is a continuing stream of samples from each distribution.

The method progressively enriches a nonparametric representation of the transportation plan, which describes how probability mass is matched between the distributions. Unlike the classic Sinkhorn algorithm, the online procedure incorporates new observations at every iteration. This continuing access to fresh samples enables consistent estimation of the underlying regularized transport distance.

The authors analyze convergence and establish an asymptotic sample-complexity result described as nearly 1/n for the iterate sequence. They validate the method using synthetic data in one through ten dimensions and real three-dimensional shape data. The contribution connects an iterative transport computation with ongoing sampling, allowing the representation to improve as more evidence arrives. Its stated estimation target is the entropy-regularized distance, which is the quantity addressed by both the algorithm and its analysis.
neurips-2020-online-sinkhorn-optimal-tra.tldr: Online Sinkhorn consistently estimates entropy-regularized transport distances by continually incorporating fresh samples from both distributions.

paragraphs: Estimating a high-dimensional mean becomes difficult when some observations are outliers. This paper studies that problem under a finite covariance assumption and, more broadly, assumptions about finite low-degree moments. The goal is to obtain strong accuracy guarantees while keeping the estimation procedure computationally efficient under these distributional conditions.

The central result concerns a stability condition used in robust statistics. The authors prove that a large fraction of the genuine observations satisfies this condition except with exponentially small failure probability. Establishing that such a stable portion exists provides the missing foundation for stronger guarantees for several recently developed estimation algorithms.

As a consequence, methods including iterative filtering and nonconvex gradient descent achieve optimal estimation errors with near-subgaussian or subgaussian rates, improving substantially on their previous analyses. The approach also yields the first computationally efficient outlier-robust mean estimator with subgaussian rates under finite covariance. The contribution shows how a sharper understanding of the reliable observations can strengthen what efficient algorithms are provably able to achieve.
neurips-2020-outlier-robust-mean-estimat.tldr: A stability theorem yields stronger robust mean-estimation guarantees, including an efficient estimator with subgaussian rates under finite covariance.

paragraphs: An image-captioning model should look at the image region associated with the word it is about to generate. The paper identifies a mismatch in common attention mechanisms: they determine where to look using information based on preceding words. This can shift attention away from the region relevant to the upcoming word, hurting both grounding and caption quality.

Prophet Attention uses future information during training to calculate target attention weights over image regions. These targets then regularize the model's ordinary attention. The mechanism resembles self-supervision because the additional guidance comes from information available within the training sequence. It is designed to be incorporated into existing captioning models.

Experiments on Flickr30k Entities and MSCOCO show consistent improvements over baselines in automatic measurements and human evaluations. The authors report state-of-the-art results on both benchmarks and first place on the online MSCOCO leaderboard under its default CIDEr-c40 ranking. These results support using future-informed training targets to improve the connection between generated words and the image regions that should support them.
neurips-2020-prophet-attention-predictin.tldr: Prophet Attention uses future information during training to guide image attention, improving reported word grounding and caption quality.

paragraphs: Understanding an image involves relationships among objects as well as the objects themselves. Human-labeled relationship datasets contain highly uneven predicate frequencies, limiting what relationship models can learn from them. This paper proposes learning visual relationships implicitly through self-supervision, without requiring ground-truth annotations of those relationships.

The method combines encodings within each modality with encodings that connect modalities. It also uses relationship probing to discover graph structure within each modality, making relationships part of the learned representation. Its self-supervised signals come from masked language modeling, contrastive learning, and distances in dependency trees. These sources provide complementary guidance for learning object features and relational structure.

The authors evaluate the method on several vision-language tasks that benefit from understanding visual relationships and report evidence of its effectiveness. The stated contribution is improved object representations together with implicitly learned relationships. This matters because it offers a way to develop useful relational information without depending on explicit visual-relationship labels whose uneven distribution constrains existing approaches.
neurips-2020-self-supervised-relationshi.tldr: Self-supervised relationship probing learns useful object features and implicit visual relationships without ground-truth visual-relationship annotations.

paragraphs: Training a generative model can be viewed as optimizing over probability distributions produced by a parameterized transformation. This paper proposes Sinkhorn Natural Gradient, or SiNG, for that setting. The method follows a steepest-descent direction defined in a probability space equipped with the Sinkhorn divergence, connecting parameter updates to the geometry of the generated distributions.

Its central computational component is the Sinkhorn information matrix. The authors derive an explicit expression for this matrix and show that it can be evaluated accurately with complexity that grows logarithmically with the requested accuracy. This addresses the practical challenge of obtaining the information needed to carry out the proposed natural-gradient updates.

When practical applications only permit Monte Carlo integration, the paper supplies an empirical matrix estimator and analyzes its stability. Experiments compare SiNG with state-of-the-art stochastic-gradient-type solvers on generative tasks and demonstrate its efficiency and effectiveness. The contribution brings together a distribution-based optimization direction, a tractable matrix calculation, and an analysis of estimation when exact integration is unavailable.
neurips-2020-sinkhorn-natural-gradient-f.tldr: SiNG optimizes generative distributions using Sinkhorn geometry, with an explicit information matrix and a stability-analyzed sampling estimator.

paragraphs: MEG and EEG source imaging seeks to determine where and when brain regions activate from noninvasive measurements. The task is a high-dimensional inference problem, and sparse regression alone leaves uncertainty about controlling false detections. Temporal dependence in both the data and noise adds another difficulty when deciding which apparent activations are statistically supported.

The authors adapt the desparsified Lasso to temporal measurements with autocorrelated noise, producing the desparsified multi-task Lasso. The underlying estimator has an asymptotically Gaussian distribution under sparsity and moderate feature-correlation assumptions. They combine it with spatially constrained clustering to reduce dimensionality, then ensemble multiple clusterings to reduce dependence on any arbitrary clustering choice.

The resulting method provides statistical guarantees and allows a tradeoff between spatial specificity and sensitivity. Simulations using realistic head geometries and evaluations on multiple MEG datasets demonstrate strong recovery performance. Its main practical contribution is a statistically principled way to threshold source maps, connecting the displayed activation regions to an inference procedure while allowing spatial resolution and detection sensitivity to be balanced.
neurips-2020-statistical-control-for-spa.tldr: An ensemble of clustered desparsified estimators enables statistically principled MEG/EEG source-map thresholding with a specificity–sensitivity tradeoff.

paragraphs: Reducing numerical precision can accelerate neural-network training, but representing gradients with very few bits creates difficulties. The available numbers must cover both the range and the fine distinctions needed during learning. This paper introduces techniques and numerical formats that enable training precision to move from eight bits to four bits.

A central component is adaptive Gradient Scaling, called Gradscale, which addresses inadequate range and resolution in quantized gradients. The authors also investigate quantization errors and theoretically analyze how bias introduced by gradient quantization affects convergence. They propose ways to mitigate that bias, linking the numerical representation to the behavior of the training process.

The techniques are evaluated across computer vision, speech, and natural language processing models. Combined with earlier methods for four-bit weights and activations, they produce accuracy losses described as nonsignificant across the studied domains. The paper also reports enabling hardware acceleration exceeding sevenfold relative to state-of-the-art FP16 systems. These findings support carefully designed gradient handling as a key component of making very low-precision training effective.
neurips-2020-ultra-low-precision-4-bit-t.tldr: Adaptive gradient scaling and bias mitigation enable four-bit training with reported nonsignificant accuracy loss and substantial hardware acceleration.

paragraphs: The geometry used to represent data determines how positions and distances are expressed. Although Euclidean space is common, other geometries can suit different structures; the paper highlights hyperbolic space for tree-like data. It proposes a broader representation space built on a pseudo-Riemannian manifold with constant nonzero curvature.

This geometry generalizes hyperbolic and spherical spaces by allowing a nondegenerate metric tensor that need not be positive definite. To make the representation usable for learning, the authors develop the necessary mathematical tools rather than only proposing a new space. They derive closed-form expressions for distances through geodesics and define a direction for decreasing an objective.

These developments extend gradient-based optimization into the proposed geometry, and the framework is applied to graph representations. The contribution is therefore both representational and computational: it supplies a different geometric setting and a way to learn within it. The stated application demonstrates where the framework is used, while the abstract's main emphasis is on establishing the geometry and optimization machinery.
neurips-2020-ultrahyperbolic-representat.tldr: The paper introduces a geometry generalizing hyperbolic and spherical spaces and develops distance and optimization tools for graph representations.

paragraphs: The paper studies Bayesian bandit problems with many available actions: the number of arms is at least the square root of the time horizon. It shows that restricting attention to a sampled subset is critical for optimal policies in this regime. Standard UCB has suboptimal regret bounds, while running UCB on a subset of square-root-horizon size is rate-optimal.

Nevertheless, numerical experiments show that this subsampled UCB explores poor arms excessively and performs worse than simple greedy policies that choose the currently best empirical arm. Related findings also appear in a contextual setting using real-world data. The authors investigate a form of free exploration connected to a tail event in the prior distribution of arm rewards.

This mechanism differs from exploration supplied by varying contexts. Using it, the authors prove rate-optimality of subsampled greedy for Bernoulli bandits when the arm count exceeds the square root of the horizon, and sublinear regret for more general distributions. The results suggest that greedy variants may be preferable in many-arm applications, while showing why asymptotic rate-optimality alone can miss practically important differences.
neurips-2020-unreasonable-effectiveness-.tldr: In many-arm bandits, greedy policies perform strongly empirically, and subsampled greedy achieves rate-optimality under the stated Bernoulli conditions.
